lecture: L23) Ocular manifestations of systemic diseases.txt
expansion:
A. Undiagnosed diabetes mellitus is correct. The thirst, polyuria and weight loss are classic symptoms of diabetes mellitus (not taken from the course material), and the sudden refractive change with a normal ocular examination supports a glucose-related lens refractive change rather than a structural eye lesion. The lecture explicitly states that diabetes mellitus has ocular complications “including refractive changes and cataract formation” (L23, page 4). Acute hyperglycaemia can alter lens hydration and refractive index, producing a transient myopic shift (not taken from the course material). This explains blurred distance vision while near vision remains relatively preserved: the refractive-errors lecture lists “Blurred distance vision” and says near vision is usually not affected in myopia (L7,8, slide 43).

B. Nuclear sclerotic cataract can cause acquired myopia: increased nuclear refractive index causes “acquired myopia,” and a nuclear cataract may give temporary “second sight” with better near reading (L18, page 6). However, this patient’s ocular structures are described as normal, and the abrupt onset with systemic diabetic symptoms makes diabetes the more likely cause.

C. Retinal detachment is not a refractive shift. Rhegmatogenous detachment more characteristically causes floaters, flashes and a peripheral “curtain” or shadow (L20, slide 11), rather than isolated new myopia with preserved near vision.

D. Presbyopia is age-related recession of the near point, so near images can no longer be focused using accommodation (L7,8, slide 73). It causes difficulty with near vision, the opposite of this presentation, and does not explain acute distance blur or diabetic symptoms.
objective: Diabetes mellitus can produce transient refractive changes, including an acute myopic shift.
